catalog_quote: Kalamang has contrastive stress that is non-predictable in disyllabic roots, but has a preference for the right edge in longer roots. ... [3.3.1.2] Stress is not related to syllable weight, position of the syllable or word class ... The fact that 129 CVCVC words in the word list have stress on the first syllable, against 190 with stress on the second syllable, proves the point that stress in disyllabic roots is not predictable. ... /ˈkol.kom/ ‘footprint’ ... /kol.ˈkom/ ‘ear’ ... [3.3.1.3] Stress never falls on the first syllable of roots with more than two syllables. The majority of such words carry stress on the penultimate syllable, but no rule can be generated since there are many counterexamples. Again, stress is not influenced by syllable weight or word class. ... The current data set clearly suggests that stress has to be on one of the last two syllables. ... [3.3.1.8] Kalamang is…

new_statements.quote: Kalamang has contrastive stress that is non-predictable in disyllabic roots, but has a preference for the right edge in longer roots. [...] In disyllabic roots, stress is completely unpredictable (§ 2.3.1.2). Roots with more than two syllables, which are less common, do not have stress on the first syllable (§ 2.3.1.3). (p. 74) — Stress never falls on the first syllable of roots with more than two syllables. The majority of words carry stress on the penultimate syllable, but no rule can be generated as counterexamples are many. Again, stress is not influenced by syllable weight or word class. (p. 78) — Kalamang is therefore best analysed as having a tendency towards a trochaic foot structure (ˈσ.σ) assigned from right to left. (p. 86)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Kalamang with an empty rule field and there are no existing stress statements, so this work supplies the placement description: contrastive, lexically unpredictable stress in disyllabic roots with a non-initial (mostly penultimate) tendency in longer and morphologically complex words, no weight sensitivity, secondary stress in compounds/reduplications, analysed as right-to-left trochaic feet.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive and lexically unpredictable in disyllabic roots (the majority of roots; (near-)minimal pairs such as /ˈkolkom/ 'footprint' vs /kolˈkom/ 'ear', /ˈtiri/ 'to run' vs /tiˈri/ 'drum'; a word-list count gives 129 CVCVC roots with initial stress against 190 with second-syllable stress). Stress is explicitly not related to syllable weight, syllable position or word class. In roots of three or more syllables stress is never initial and is usually penultimate, but final stress is common enough that no rule can be stated; the only candidate antepenultimate root is a probable loan place name /tuˈburasap/. Words carrying suffixes or enclitics generally take penultimate stress (stress shifts to the last root syllable before the suffix/enclitic; final-stressed roots keep it; monosyllabic roots keep it), so the author analyses the language as tending towards a right-to-left trochaic foot (ˈσ.σ). A phonological word carries one main stress, cued primarily by intensity, secondarily by length, and thirdly by high pitch. The language has no lexical tone; the intonation system uses an H* pitch accent on the stressed syllable of content words (§2.3.3, p. 88ff.). Length is non-contrastive (§2.3.2, p. 87).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Secondary stress appears in some compounds (mainly numerals) and in reduplicated words with four or more syllables' (p. 75); it 'has the same indicators as primary stress, but they are weaker', e.g. /ˌsiŋaˈsiŋat/ 'ant' (p. 77); compound numerals show (σ)σˈσσˌσ patterns and secondary stress on non-final parts, e.g. 70 [put.ˌra.man.ˈda.lin] (pp. 83-84); fully reduplicated disyllables e.g. [ˌga.ruŋ.ˈga.ruŋ] 'to talk (durative)' (p. 85).
new_statements.exceptions: Many: (i) disyllabic roots with final stress are unexplained by the trochaic analysis; (ii) affixed/encliticised words usually penultimate but with 'many exceptions' (e.g. /na.kal-ˈun=bon=at/, /pa.tin=ˈnin=ten/); disyllabic clitics =taet, =saet and the suffix -mahap give unpredictable placement; (iii) the volitional enclitic =kin attracts stress ([tur.ˈkin], [ko.met.ˈkin]) but not always from non-adjacent syllables; (iv) the reciprocal proclitic nau= sometimes carries primary stress though not penultimate ([ˈna.u=ka.ha.ˌman]); (v) compounds with kor/tan show no rule in disyllables; some compounds keep two primary stresses as two phonological words; (vi) compound numerals are penultimate even when the simple numeral is final-stressed (karuok [ka.ˈrok] vs putkaruok [put.ˈka.rok]); (vii) possible antepenult loan root /tuˈburasap/ 'Tuburuasa'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Kalamang (ISO kgv, aka Karas) of the Karas Islands, Fakfak regency, West Papua, Indonesia, from the author's own fieldwork 2015-2019 (villages Mas and Antalisa, corpus mainly Mas); no dialect distinction is drawn in the stress description.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (lexical/contrastive stress, unpredictable in disyllabic roots, confined to the last two syllables in longer roots, weight irrelevant, right edge, trochaic R-to-L tendency) rests on a 2022 open-access LangSci reference grammar by the language's sole modern describer, with instrumental figures and wordlist counts; every fragment of the deciding quote and the domain quote is verbatim in the text we hold at the stated sections/pages. Glottolog lists no non-Visser description; the author's ORCID list shows no dedicated prosody paper; the 2016 MA thesis (downloaded to gives the same analysis with smaller counts. Nothing better exists and nothing suggests a reclassify.
